objectives: Explain the digital workflow of CAD/CAM dentistry, intraoral scanning, and 3D printing.
Describe cone-beam CT, dental lasers, and AI-assisted radiographic diagnosis of caries and bone loss.
Outline the principles of teledentistry, regenerative/stem-cell dentistry, and minimally invasive dentistry.

slides.title: CAD/CAM, intraoral scanning, and 3D printing
slides.body:
**Digital dentistry** replaces analog impressions, casts, and hand-fabrication with computerised capture, design, and manufacture. Its centrepiece is **CAD/CAM** — **Computer-Aided Design / Computer-Aided Manufacturing** — which lets a dentist design a restoration on screen and machine it from a solid block.

The pioneering system was **CEREC** ("Chairside Economical Restoration of Esthetic Ceramics"), conceived by **Werner Mörmann** and the engineer **Marco Brandestini** at the **University of Zurich**, who delivered the **first CAD/CAM ceramic inlay milled and placed at the chairside in 1985**. A modern CEREC or comparable workflow has three stages: **digitise** the prepared tooth, **design** the restoration in software, and **mill** it from a ceramic or composite block (using lithium disilicate or zirconia, as covered earlier) — often in a single appointment, eliminating the temporary crown and second visit.

The digitising step uses an **intraoral scanner (IOS)**, a wand-shaped optical device that projects light and reconstructs a 3D surface model of the teeth and gums, replacing messy alginate or polyvinyl-siloxane impression materials. Leading systems include the **CEREC Primescan/Omnicam**, the **3Shape TRIOS**, and the **Align iTero**. Scans are stored as **STL** or **PLY** point-cloud meshes that flow into design and manufacturing software.

Manufacture is either **subtractive** or **additive**. Subtractive **milling** carves the object from a block, wasting material but excellent for dense ceramics. **Additive manufacturing — 3D printing** — builds objects layer by layer and is revolutionising the dental laboratory. The dominant dental printing technologies are **stereolithography (SLA)** and **digital light processing (DLP)**, which cure liquid photopolymer resin with light, and increasingly **material jetting**. Dentists 3D-print **study models, surgical guides for implant placement, clear-aligner models, temporary crowns, denture bases, and night guards**, with printed permanent restorations and even bioprinting on the horizon. Together, the **intraoral scan → CAD design → milling or printing** pipeline forms the digital backbone on which the rest of this lesson's frontier technologies build.

slides.title: Cone-beam CT, dental lasers, and AI radiograph diagnosis
slides.body:
Three technologies are reshaping how dentists see and treat the mouth.

**Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)** is a 3D imaging method introduced for dentistry around **1998** (the **NewTom** scanner by **Quantitative Radiology** in Italy, with foundational work by **Mozzo, Tacconi, and colleagues**). Unlike a fan-beam medical CT, a CBCT rotates a **cone-shaped X-ray beam** once around the head, capturing a volume that is reconstructed into thin slices and 3D models. CBCT delivers a **far lower radiation dose** than conventional CT while giving the dentist undistorted, measurable 3D anatomy. It is invaluable for **implant planning** (measuring bone height and locating the **inferior alveolar nerve canal** and **maxillary sinus**), **endodontics** (finding missed canals and assessing apical lesions), impacted teeth, and surgical planning. Because dose still exceeds a 2D radiograph, its use is governed by the **ALARA principle** ("As Low As Reasonably Achievable").

**Dental lasers** (Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation) deliver concentrated light energy tuned to specific tissues. **Soft-tissue lasers** (such as **diode** and **Nd:YAG** lasers) cut, coagulate, and decontaminate gum tissue with minimal bleeding, useful in periodontal and minor surgical procedures. **Hard-tissue lasers** — chiefly the **erbium** family (**Er:YAG** and **Er,Cr:YSGG**), whose wavelengths (around **2780–2940 nm**) are strongly absorbed by water and hydroxyapatite — can ablate enamel and dentin to remove decay, sometimes reducing the need for the drill and local anaesthetic. Lasers are also used for **caries detection** (the **DIAGNOdent** fluorescence device) and **photobiomodulation**.

Most transformative is **artificial intelligence in radiographic diagnosis**. **Convolutional neural networks (CNNs)** and other **deep-learning** models, trained on large sets of labelled radiographs, now assist in detecting **interproximal and occlusal caries**, measuring **periodontal/alveolar bone loss**, identifying periapical lesions, and charting teeth automatically. Commercial systems such as **Pearl (Second Opinion)** and **Overjet** received **U.S. FDA clearance** (around 2021–2022) for AI-assisted detection of caries and bone loss on bitewing and periapical radiographs, acting as a "second pair of eyes" that flags lesions the clinician might overlook. Studies show AI can match or exceed average clinician sensitivity for early caries, though human oversight remains essential and questions of bias, validation, and liability are actively debated. AI is also entering **CBCT segmentation**, **orthodontic landmark detection** for cephalometrics, and treatment-outcome prediction.

slides.title: Teledentistry, regenerative dentistry, and minimally invasive care
slides.body:
Beyond hardware, three movements are redefining the philosophy and reach of dental care.

**Teledentistry** uses telecommunications to deliver dental advice, triage, and monitoring at a distance. It encompasses **"store-and-forward"** (a patient or hygienist transmits photos, scans, and records for later expert review), **live videoconferencing** (real-time consultation), and **remote monitoring** (for example, patients photographing aligner progress with apps like **Dental Monitoring**). The **COVID-19 pandemic of 2020** dramatically accelerated adoption, and the **American Dental Association (ADA)** issued specific teledentistry policy and billing (CDT) codes. Teledentistry improves access for rural and underserved populations, nursing-home residents, and school-based programs, while screening which patients truly need an in-person visit — though it cannot replace hands-on examination and treatment.

**Regenerative and stem-cell dentistry** aims to **biologically rebuild** dental tissues rather than replace them with artificial materials. Building on the discovery of **dental pulp stem cells (DPSCs)** by **Songtao Shi and Stan Gronthos around 2000**, researchers have identified several oral stem-cell sources: **stem cells from human exfoliated deciduous teeth (SHED)**, **stem cells of the apical papilla (SCAP)**, **periodontal ligament stem cells (PDLSCs)**, and **dental follicle progenitor cells**. The field pursues **whole-tooth bioengineering**, **pulp regeneration** (linked to the regenerative endodontics covered earlier), **periodontal tissue regeneration** using scaffolds and growth factors, and the use of **enamel matrix derivative** and **bone morphogenetic proteins**. Some jurisdictions now bank extracted teeth as a source of autologous stem cells. Although whole-tooth regeneration remains experimental, periodontal and pulp regeneration are moving steadily toward the clinic.

Unifying these advances is the philosophy of **minimally invasive dentistry (MID)**, sometimes called **minimal intervention dentistry**, championed by figures such as **Graham Mount** and the **FDI World Dental Federation**. MID reframes caries as a manageable disease and emphasises **early detection** (ICDAS, laser fluorescence, AI), **prevention and remineralisation** (fluoride, sealants, **silver diamine fluoride (SDF)** to arrest decay without drilling), and, when intervention is needed, **conserving the maximum healthy tooth structure** — for example with the **atraumatic restorative treatment (ART)** technique and small adhesive composite or glass-ionomer restorations. The trajectory of digital dentistry — precise diagnosis, conservative treatment, and biological regeneration — represents the convergence of all the materials, anatomy, and disease principles studied across this learning path.

question.question: What does CAD/CAM enable in dentistry, and which system pioneered chairside CAD/CAM ceramic restorations in 1985?
options: Remote video consultations; the Dental Monitoring app.
On-screen design and machine fabrication of restorations; the CEREC system developed by Mörmann and Brandestini.
Detection of caries with fluorescent light; the DIAGNOdent device.
3D imaging of the jaw with a cone-shaped X-ray beam; the NewTom scanner.
question.explanation: CAD/CAM (Computer-Aided Design / Computer-Aided Manufacturing) lets the dentist design a restoration digitally and mill it from a block, pioneered by the CEREC system of Werner Mörmann and Marco Brandestini, which produced the first chairside CAD/CAM ceramic inlay in 1985. Option A describes teledentistry, option C describes laser caries detection, and option D describes CBCT — different technologies.

hints: CAD/CAM is about designing and milling restorations.
The pioneering system's name abbreviates 'Chairside Economical Restoration of Esthetic Ceramics'.
slides.workedSolution: CAD/CAM stands for Computer-Aided Design / Computer-Aided Manufacturing. In dentistry it allows a prepared tooth to be digitised, the restoration designed on screen, and the final crown, inlay, or onlay milled from a ceramic block, often in a single visit. The pioneering system was CEREC, developed by Werner Mörmann and Marco Brandestini at the University of Zurich, which delivered the first chairside CAD/CAM ceramic inlay in 1985. Teledentistry, laser fluorescence detection, and CBCT are separate technologies.

question.question: What is the main advantage of cone-beam CT (CBCT) over conventional medical CT for dental use?
options: It uses no ionising radiation at all.
It provides 3D imaging at a substantially lower radiation dose than conventional CT.
It can only image soft tissue, never bone.
It eliminates the need for any 2D radiographs in all cases.
question.explanation: CBCT rotates a cone-shaped X-ray beam once around the head to reconstruct a 3D volume at a much lower radiation dose than fan-beam medical CT, while giving undistorted, measurable anatomy. It does use ionising radiation (option A is false), it images hard tissue (bone and teeth) very well (option C is false), and because its dose still exceeds a 2D film, it is reserved for cases that need 3D information rather than replacing all 2D imaging (option D).

hints: Compare the radiation dose to a regular medical CT scan.
It still uses X-rays, so it is not dose-free.
slides.workedSolution: Cone-beam computed tomography captures a 3D volume by rotating a cone-shaped X-ray beam once around the patient's head, which is reconstructed into slices and 3D models. Its principal advantage over conventional fan-beam medical CT is a substantially lower radiation dose while still providing undistorted, measurable three-dimensional anatomy of bone and teeth. This makes it ideal for implant planning, complex endodontics, and surgical assessment. Because its dose still exceeds that of a 2D radiograph, its use follows the ALARA principle and is reserved for cases that genuinely require 3D data.

question.question: An AI caries-detection model is evaluated on 200 true caries lesions and correctly identifies 170 of them. Compute the model's sensitivity (true positive rate) as a percentage to one decimal place.
A practice is deciding whether to adopt AI radiograph analysis software
question.prompt: A dental practice is considering adopting an FDA-cleared AI system such as Overjet or Pearl that flags caries and alveolar bone loss on bitewing radiographs. The senior dentist worries the AI will either miss lesions or over-diagnose and lead to unnecessary drilling, and asks how it should be used responsibly. Drawing on the concepts of sensitivity, the role of AI as a 'second pair of eyes,' minimally invasive dentistry, and clinician oversight, explain the appropriate role of AI in diagnosis, the risks of both false negatives and false positives, and why human judgment must remain central.

question.question: Which of the following best captures the philosophy of minimally invasive dentistry (MID)?
options: Extracting and replacing any tooth with even minor decay to prevent future problems.
Early detection, prevention and remineralisation, and conserving maximum healthy tooth structure when intervention is needed.
Always preferring full crowns over fillings for durability.
Avoiding all use of fluoride and sealants.
question.explanation: Minimally invasive (minimal intervention) dentistry treats caries as a manageable disease, emphasising early detection, prevention and remineralisation, arresting agents such as silver diamine fluoride, and preserving as much sound tooth as possible when restoration is necessary. Aggressive extraction (A) and routine crowning (C) are the opposite philosophy, and MID actively uses fluoride and sealants, contradicting option D.

hints: The clue is in the name: minimal intervention, maximum preservation.
It favours prevention and remineralisation over drilling.
slides.workedSolution: Minimally invasive dentistry, championed by Graham Mount and the FDI World Dental Federation, reframes dental caries as a manageable, largely preventable disease rather than something that must be drilled out. Its pillars are early detection (using ICDAS, laser fluorescence, and AI), prevention and remineralisation (fluoride, sealants, silver diamine fluoride to arrest lesions), and, when a restoration is genuinely needed, conserving the maximum amount of healthy tooth structure with small adhesive restorations. Aggressive extraction or routine full-coverage crowns and abandoning fluoride all run counter to this philosophy.
